newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Minor panic but little damage from HK bourse glitch.
newsitem.headline: Minor panic but little damage from HK bourse glitch.

text.p: Hong Kong's stock market was thrown into confusion on Thursday after the bourse's computer erroneously showed the blue-chip Hang Seng Index had plunged nearly four percent at the open.

"People got pretty alarmed when they saw the market was down over 500 points, but it seems that different screens were giving different information," said Howard Gorges, director at South China Brokerage.
"So I think hurried checking showed the computers were wrong, that prices weren't nearly so bad," he said.

Figures on Teletext, the exchange's computer-based information system that supplies stock and index quotations as well as company and exchange announcements, showed the blue-chip index off about 515 points in the opening minutes of trade.
In fact, the index fell only 158.37 points at its lowest point, the firm that calculates the index later said. It ended the day down 136.32 points at 13,053.28 on profit-taking.
The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong said the problem arose because "a technical defect" caused its computer to generate the wrong closing figures for the previous day's trade.
It did not give details of the defect but said in a statement that it was "conducting a review of the incident".

Alec Tsui, deputy chief executive in charge of the bourse's operation services, issued a statement in late morning advising members to ignore the index's previous closing price shown on its Teletext page due to a technical malfunction with its Automatic Order Matching and Execution System.

While the exchange quickly listed the correct previous closing levels of all indices and stocks at the bottoms of their respective Teletext pages, price-change figures calculated based on exchange data remained wrong in many systems.
Banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc was shown finishing the day up HK$23.297 at HK$156.50. The closing figure was right but the share was actually down HK$2.50.
Despite the confusion, traders said the numbers were so out of line that they quickly figured out something was wrong, resulting only in minor inconvenience.
"Prices were more than 10 spreads different, HK$10 different for every stock," said a dealer with a local brokerage.
"But there was no big question of it affecting the market because we usually wait till things are clear before acting -- wait for clients to understand the prices better before acting," she said.
"I didn't do much for several minutes. That was all."
She said she incurred little loss.
"All trades were done at correct prices," said Antony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas. "Only the historical information on the screen was wrong."
Stock exchange council member Syed Bokhary said the impact was unlikely to be major since the error was so obvious.
"It was fortunate that the errors were so big. When the prices are wrong by so many spreads, (the errors) are obvious and people shouldn't make mistakes," Bokhary said.
"But the deals executed mistakenly by those who were careless should be able to be cancelled."

The exchange said in a statement it endeavours to ensure the accuracy and reliability of information it provides but does not guarantee it and accepts no liability for any loss or damage arising from any inaccuracies or omissions.
